question: How is Go's garbage collector best described?
options: A generational, moving/compacting collector like the JVM
A concurrent, non-generational, non-moving tricolor mark-and-sweep collector with two brief stop-the-world pauses per cycle
A reference-counting collector that frees objects immediately
A stop-the-world collector that pauses the program for the entire mark and sweep
explanation: Go's GC is a concurrent, non-generational, non-moving tricolor mark-and-sweep collector. It does most work alongside the program with only two sub-millisecond stop-the-world points per cycle (mark setup and mark termination). Because it is non-moving, object addresses stay stable.

question:
With default GOGC=100 and a live heap of 40 MB after a cycle, roughly when does the next GC trigger?

// heap goal = liveHeap * (1 + GOGC/100)
options: At ~40 MB (immediately)
At ~80 MB (the heap doubles)
At ~140 MB
Never, until GOMEMLIMIT is hit
explanation: heap goal = 40 * (1 + 100/100) = 80 MB. GOGC=100 means the next cycle triggers when the heap has grown by 100% (doubled) over the live set from the previous cycle.

options: Nothing is wrong — the GC frees old entries automatically
Memory grows without bound; the GC cannot reclaim map entries that are still referenced (a logical leak)
It panics on the second call
The map auto-evicts the oldest keys
explanation: Every entry is still referenced by the map, so it is 'live' to the GC and never collected. The garbage collector reclaims only unreachable objects, so this is a logical leak. The fix is a bounded/evicting cache (LRU, TTL) or deleting entries when done.

question: A handler calls runtime.GC() at the end of every request to 'keep memory low'. What is wrong with this?
options: runtime.GC() does not exist
Forcing a full collection per request runs the GC far more often than the pacer would, burning CPU and adding latency — the opposite of the goal
It only works when cgo is enabled
It leaks a goroutine on every call
explanation: Forcing a full collection on every request makes the GC run far more frequently than the pacer would schedule, burning CPU and adding latency. Let the pacer time collections; tune GOGC/GOMEMLIMIT or reduce allocations instead of calling runtime.GC() manually.

question: In a container with a 1 GiB hard memory limit, what is the recommended way to keep the GC from letting the process get OOM-killed?
options: debug.SetGCPercent(900)
debug.SetMemoryLimit(900 << 20) — a soft limit set below the hard limit
Call runtime.GC() in a loop
debug.FreeOSMemory() on every request
explanation: GOMEMLIMIT / debug.SetMemoryLimit sets a soft byte cap; setting it to ~900 MiB leaves headroom under the 1 GiB hard limit so the runtime collects more aggressively before the OOM killer fires. SetGCPercent tunes a growth ratio, not a byte limit, and the other calls force one-off collections.

options: Re-slicing copies the whole backing array, doubling memory
The backing array still holds pointers to every popped *Job, so those objects remain reachable and the GC cannot free them
q.items[1:] allocates a new slice header on the heap each call
Pop must call runtime.GC() to release the popped element
explanation: Re-slicing only advances the slice header's pointer and shrinks its length; the backing array still references every popped *Job, keeping them reachable through the slice's capacity so the GC never frees them. Nil out the popped slot (q.items[0] = nil) before advancing, and compact the array periodically.
